source.title: Dissociation as a disorder of integration - On the footsteps of Pierre Janet

confidence_rationale: Master anchor for the dissociative pole: puts Janet's clinical account of dissociation as disrupted integration into a modern frame, and its own taxonomy (compartmentalization vs. detachment vs. structural dissociation) maps directly onto two structurally distinct ways MECH-524's restrictive trigger could fail, rather than the single undifferentiated 'stuck too restrictive' pole the claim's notes currently name. Confidence held at moderate because the paper's own three-level neuronal integration proposal is explicitly offered as hypothesis, not established mechanism.
failure_signatures: A dissociative agent failure mode may not be a single unitary 'trigger too restrictive' phenomenon: Janet/Scalabrini's own clinical taxonomy separates compartmentalization (content never captured or made accessible -- amnesia-like) from detachment (content present but subjectively estranged and not engaged -- depersonalization-like). If the analogy holds, MECH-524's restrictive pole should itself split into a snapshot-never-captured failure and a snapshot-captured-but-never-reseeded failure, with potentially different falsifiers for each.

The paper explicitly states the exact neuronal mechanisms leading from disrupted integration to the different dissociative symptom clusters 'remain unclear.' Grounding MECH-524's dissociative pole in this literature borrows a clinical taxonomy and a hypothesis about levels of integration, not a validated neural mechanism -- premature to treat the three-level (regional/network/global) proposal as anything more than a structural analogy.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Janet described dissociation as an altered state of consciousness manifested in disrupted integration of psychological functions. Clinically this disruption comprises compartmentalization symptoms (amnesia), detachment symptoms (depersonalization/derealization), and structural dissociation of personality with altered sense of self. The authors propose three neuronal mechanisms of dynamic integration operating at different brain levels -- temporo-spatial binding (regional), synchronization (network), and globalization (global level) -- and suggest these different levels of disrupted integration map onto the different symptomatic manifestations of dissociation.
mapping.ree_translation: Grounds MECH-524's dissociative-loss-of-thread pole with a two-way split rather than treating it as one phenomenon. A regional/binding-level failure is REE's analogue of compartmentalization/amnesia: the interruption_snapshot's content (z_world/z_self/z_goal/CEM-stage/rule-arbitration-weights) is never captured or bound together at interruption time, so there is nothing to reseed even if the trigger later fires correctly. A network/synchronization-level failure is REE's analogue of detachment/depersonalization: the snapshot IS captured, and the spare-compute or sleep-entry trigger DOES fire, but the reseeding coupling into MECH-293's probes or MECH-285's replay never engages -- capacity is present and free, but disconnected from the specific content it should act on. MECH-524's own notes currently describe only the second shape ('never gets actively resumed... indistinguishable from an entry that was never worth resuming'); this literature suggests the first shape (capture failure) is a distinct, equally clinically-grounded failure mode worth naming separately in a future design pass.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Human clinical-population theoretical synthesis with preliminary fMRI support for the authors' own dynamic-integration model, not a mechanistic claim about an artificial world-model agent. The three-level (regional/network/global) integration hierarchy is the authors' own proposal, not an independently established fact, and REE has no validated multi-level integration hierarchy to test the analogy against -- only the STRUCTURE of the failure taxonomy (capture failure vs. coupling failure) transfers, not any specific neural implementation claim.
mapping.source_context: Theoretical/conceptual review putting Janet's 19th-century clinical account into a modern neuroscience frame, drawing on preliminary fMRI data supporting the authors' own dynamic temporo-spatial integration model; not a primary empirical study with an REE-relevant resumption task.

confidence_components.notes: Peer-reviewed, reputable field-specific journal, theoretical review with preliminary empirical support behind its own proposed model. Mapping fidelity moderate: the abstract structure (integration failure producing distinguishable phenotypes) maps cleanly onto splitting MECH-524's restrictive pole into two sub-modes, but REE has no literal multi-level integration hierarchy to validate this against. Transfer risk moderate-high: human clinical psychopathology to artificial agent architecture is a substantial hop, compounded on top of the paper's own hop from psychology to neuroscience.
